findings.summary: Universal Serial Bus (USB) is an industry standard for digital data transmission and power delivery between electronics, originally designed to replace legacy computer ports. It defines physical interfaces and communication protocols between hosts and peripheral devices via hubs. Over time, USB evolved through multiple specification generations, each adding higher signaling rates and new capabilities while maintaining backward compatibility with earlier versions. The latest standard, USB4, uses the USB-C connector and supports tunneling of multiple protocols including PCIe and DisplayPort, with dynamic speed sharing across a single physical interface. USB also provides power delivery, with recent versions supporting up to 240 watts via the USB Power Delivery specification.

mechanisms.title: Physical Interface and Protocol Specification
mechanisms.explanation: USB specifies the architecture of physical interfaces and communication protocols for data and power transfer between hosts, hubs, and peripheral devices. The standard defines connector types (Type-A, Type-B, Type-C) and the associated signaling rates and pin configurations required for operation.

mechanisms.title: Backward Compatibility and Speed Negotiation
mechanisms.explanation: Each newer USB specification maintains backward compatibility with previous versions, typically resulting in reduced signaling rates and limited power capabilities when older devices are connected. Newer specifications often support multiple operation modes (e.g., Gen 1×1, Gen 2×1, Gen 2×2) that are selected based on connected hardware capabilities and cable type.
